_README: Typical values for Minnesota. Height is mature height in cultivation; bloom is month range in the Twin Cities (a week or two later up north, earlier in the far south); sun/moisture/soil are the growing conditions the species tolerates in MN, not its full continental range. Family comes from GBIF and is filled in mechanically by scripts/fill-quick-facts.py - do not hand-edit family here. Animals carry a different field set (type/status/season/needs/where) because bloom time and soil are meaningless for a bee.

american-basswood.wildlife: Nectar-rich flowers worked heavily by bees; seeds eaten by birds

american-cranberrybush-viburnum.wildlife: Red fruit persists into winter for waxwings and robins

american-elm.wildlife: Larval host for question mark and comma butterflies; early seed for birds

american-hazelnut.wildlife: Nuts for squirrels, jays and grouse; thicket nesting cover

amsonia.wildlife: Early nectar for bees; brilliant gold fall color

aromatic-aster.wildlife: Critical late nectar for bees and migrating monarchs

arrowhead.wildlife: Tubers eaten by ducks and muskrats

balsam-fir.wildlife: Winter cover and browse; seed for crossbills and red squirrels

beaked-hazelnut.wildlife: Nuts for grouse and squirrels; understory cover

bearberry.wildlife: Evergreen mat; berries hold through winter for birds

big-bluestem.wildlife: Larval host for several skippers; heavy nesting cover

bittersweet.wildlife: Orange fruit for birds. Native - do not confuse with invasive Oriental Bittersweet

black-ash.wildlife: Keystone of black-ash swamps; now devastated by emerald ash borer

black-cherry.wildlife: Host to over 400 caterpillar species; fruit for birds and mammals

black-eyed-susan.wildlife: Long bloom for bees and butterflies; seed for goldfinches

black-walnut.wildlife: Nuts for squirrels; roots release juglone, which suppresses some neighbors

blazing-star.wildlife: The strongest monarch magnet in the Minnesota palette

bloodroot.wildlife: Ant-dispersed seed; very early pollen for emerging queens

blue-beech.wildlife: Understory tree; seed for birds; sinewy muscle-like bark

blue-cohosh.wildlife: Blue seed taken by birds; indicator of undisturbed woods

blue-flag-iris.wildlife: Shoreline stabilizer; worked by bumble bees and hummingbirds

blue-joint-grass.wildlife: Dominant wet-meadow grass; nesting cover for marsh birds

blue-stemmed-goldenrod.wildlife: One of the few shade-tolerant goldenrods; late woodland nectar

boneset.wildlife: Swarmed by small native bees, wasps and flies

bottlebrush-sedge.wildlife: Wetland restoration workhorse; seed for waterfowl

boxelder.wildlife: Fast floodplain colonizer; seed for birds; host to boxelder bugs

broad-leaved-cattail.wildlife: Marsh-bird nesting cover. Native, but aggressive where water levels are stabilized

buffalograss.wildlife: Short-grass prairie sod; at the eastern edge of its range in Minnesota

bunchberry.wildlife: Red berries for grouse and thrushes; carpets northern conifer floors

bur-oak.wildlife: Keystone species - acorns feed dozens of animals, host to 400+ caterpillars; fire-resistant bark

butterfly-milkweed.wildlife: Monarch host plant; the orange one, and the driest-site milkweed

canada-goldenrod.wildlife: Major late nectar source. Native but rhizomatous - spreads hard in gardens

canada-wild-rye.wildlife: Fast-establishing nurse grass for new prairie seedings

cardinal-flower.wildlife: Pollinated almost entirely by ruby-throated hummingbirds

chokecherry.wildlife: Fruit for dozens of bird species; host to many caterpillars

christmas-fern.wildlife: Evergreen through winter; shelter for ground invertebrates

closed-gentian.wildlife: Flowers never open - only bumble bees are strong enough to force them

common-buckthorn.wildlife: INVASIVE. Leafs out early and holds late, shading out natives; berries cause bird diarrhea, spreading seed

common-milkweed.wildlife: Primary monarch host in Minnesota; powerfully fragrant, heavily visited

common-ragweed.wildlife: Native annual; seed is major winter bird food. The real cause of hay fever, not goldenrod

compass-plant.wildlife: Leaves orient north-south; taproot reaches 15 ft; seed for finches

coontail.wildlife: Cover for young fish; food for waterfowl

cranberry.wildlife: Bog specialist; fruit for birds; the commercial cranberry species

culvers-root.wildlife: White candelabra spikes worked by many bees; strong vertical structure

cup-plant.wildlife: Paired leaves hold rainwater that birds drink from; seed for finches

dogbane.wildlife: Nectar for many insects; historically a cordage fiber. Toxic to livestock

dotted-blazing-star.wildlife: Driest-site liatris; deep taproot; late nectar

dutchmans-breeches.wildlife: Spring ephemeral; pollinated by queen bumble bees; ant-dispersed seed

echinacea.wildlife: Narrow-leaved coneflower of dry prairie; seed for goldfinches

elderberry.wildlife: Fruit taken by more than 40 bird species; flat flower heads feed many insects

evening-primrose.wildlife: Opens at dusk for moths; seed heads feed winter birds

false-blue-indigo.wildlife: Nitrogen fixer; long-lived; larval host for several sulphurs and duskywings

false-solomons-seal.wildlife: Terminal flower plume, then red berries for birds

fox-sedge.wildlife: Core bioswale and rain-garden sedge; seed for waterfowl

garlic-mustard.wildlife: INVASIVE. Poisons soil fungi that native trees depend on; a single plant sets thousands of seeds

glossy-buckthorn.wildlife: INVASIVE. Wetland counterpart to common buckthorn; overruns fens and bogs

golden-alexanders.wildlife: Larval host for black swallowtail; critical early-season nectar for small bees

goldthread.wildlife: Bog and conifer-swamp groundcover; thread-like golden roots

gray-dogwood.wildlife: White berries on red pedicels - a fall signature; heavy bird use

gray-goldenrod.wildlife: Well-behaved dry-site goldenrod; late nectar without the aggression

great-blue-lobelia.wildlife: Bumble-bee pollinated; the blue companion to cardinal flower

green-ash.wildlife: Once the standard boulevard tree; now devastated by emerald ash borer

harebell.wildlife: Nodding blue bells on cliffs and dry banks; long bloom for small bees

heavy-sedge.wildlife: Dry-prairie sedge; early green-up before the warm-season grasses

hepatica.wildlife: Among the very first woodland flowers; leaves overwinter

hog-peanut.wildlife: Nitrogen fixer; underground seeds eaten by mammals and historically by people

indian-grass.wildlife: Golden-bronze plumes; nesting cover; one of the big four tallgrasses

ironweed.wildlife: Intense purple; heavy butterfly and bee use in late summer

ironwood.wildlife: Hop-like fruit for grouse and finches; extremely hard wood

jack-in-the-pulpit.wildlife: Fungus-gnat pollinated; red berry cluster for birds; changes sex year to year

japanese-barberry.wildlife: INVASIVE. Dense thickets raise humidity and are linked to higher deer-tick densities

jerusalem-artichoke.wildlife: Native sunflower with edible tubers; very late nectar. Spreads aggressively

joe-pye-weed.wildlife: Big dusty-pink heads; one of the best butterfly plants for wet ground

june-grass.wildlife: Cool-season prairie bunchgrass; flowers before the warm-season grasses start

kentucky-bluegrass.wildlife: NON-NATIVE. The standard lawn grass; displaces native sod in unmanaged prairie

labrador-tea.wildlife: Bog shrub with fuzzy rust-colored leaf undersides; long a northern tea plant

lady-fern.wildlife: Lacy and adaptable; shelter for amphibians and ground insects

lake-sedge.wildlife: Forms broad colonies at lake edges; muskrat food, marsh-bird cover

large-flowered-trillium.wildlife: Ant-dispersed seed; takes 7-10 years to first flower. Never pick - it can kill the plant

large-leaved-aster.wildlife: Broad basal leaves carpet northern woods; late shade nectar

lead-plant.wildlife: Nitrogen fixer; roots reach 15 ft; indicator of high-quality remnant prairie

leafy-spurge.wildlife: INVASIVE, state noxious weed. Roots reach 20 ft; milky sap burns skin and deters grazing

leatherleaf.wildlife: Forms the floating bog mat; very early bloom for emerging queen bumble bees

leatherwood.wildlife: Bark so pliable it can be tied in a knot; very early nectar

little-bluestem.wildlife: Host to several skippers; copper winter color; the most-planted native grass

maidenhair-fern.wildlife: Whorled fronds on black wiry stems; a Minnesota native woodland fern

maple-leaved-viburnum.wildlife: Shade-tolerant shrub; black fruit for birds; pink-purple fall color

marsh-blazing-star.wildlife: The wet-ground liatris; strong butterfly and bee draw

marsh-marigold.wildlife: Blazing yellow in early spring seeps; very early pollen

moonseed.wildlife: Fruit for birds. TOXIC to people - looks like wild grape but the seed is crescent-shaped

nannyberry.wildlife: Sweet blue-black fruit persists into winter; excellent small native tree

narrow-leaved-cattail.wildlife: NON-NATIVE and aggressive; hybridizes with native cattail to form invasive stands

nettle.wildlife: Larval host for red admiral and question mark butterflies. Stinging hairs

new-england-aster.wildlife: Deep purple; among the most valuable late-season nectar plants in Minnesota

ninebark.wildlife: Exfoliating bark for winter interest; flowers worked by many small bees

nodding-trillium.wildlife: Flower hangs below the leaves; ant-dispersed seed

northern-white-cedar.wildlife: Critical deer winter shelter and browse; cliff specimens can exceed 1,000 years

oriental-bittersweet.wildlife: INVASIVE. Strangles and topples mature trees; hybridizes with native American bittersweet

ostrich-fern.wildlife: Fiddleheads are the edible ones; spreads by runners into large colonies

pagoda-dogwood.wildlife: Distinct horizontal tiered branching; blue fruit on red stems for birds

pale-purple-coneflower.wildlife: Drooping narrow petals; the dry-prairie coneflower; seed for goldfinches

pasque-flower.wildlife: Minnesota's earliest prairie bloom, often through snow; feathery seed plumes

pennsylvania-sedge.wildlife: The native dry-shade lawn substitute; forms soft flowing carpets

pickerelweed.wildlife: Blue spikes worked hard by bumble bees; seed for ducks

pin-oak.wildlife: Acorns for waterfowl and mammals; lower branches sweep downward

poison-ivy.wildlife: Native; berries are important winter bird food. Urushiol causes severe rash - leaves of three

porcelain-berry.wildlife: INVASIVE. Speckled blue and purple fruit spreads by birds; smothers shrubs and small trees

porcupine-grass.wildlife: Sharp awned seeds drill themselves into the soil; remnant dry-prairie indicator

prairie-blazing-star.wildlife: Tallest liatris; dense wands of purple; heavy monarch and bumble bee use

prairie-dropseed.wildlife: Fine fountain-like mounds; seed smells of coriander; slow but very long-lived

prairie-phlox.wildlife: Fragrant pink; nectar tube suits butterflies and moths

prairie-sedge.wildlife: Calcareous fen and wet-meadow sedge; early cover

prairie-smoke.wildlife: Nodding pink buds, then unmistakable feathery seed plumes; very early bumble bee forage

prairie-turnip.wildlife: Nitrogen fixer; starchy root was a staple food for Dakota and other Plains peoples

purple-coneflower.wildlife: Long bloom for butterflies and bees; leave the seed heads for winter goldfinches

purple-loosestrife.wildlife: INVASIVE, state prohibited. One plant makes over 2 million seeds; converts marshes to monoculture

purple-prairie-clover.wildlife: Nitrogen fixer; the blooming ring climbs the head; excellent bee plant

pussytoes.wildlife: Larval host for American lady butterfly; silver mat for poor dry soil

quaking-aspen.wildlife: Host to 300+ caterpillar species; grouse and beaver food; clones can cover acres

rattlesnake-master.wildlife: Yucca-like leaves and spiky globes; supports specialist wasps and beetles

red-berried-elder.wildlife: Red fruit in midsummer, well before other elders; heavy bird use

red-maple.wildlife: Among the earliest pollen sources of the year; brilliant red fall color

red-oak.wildlife: Fast-growing keystone oak; acorns mature in two years; host to hundreds of caterpillars

red-osier-dogwood.wildlife: Brilliant red winter stems; white fruit for birds; superb streambank stabilizer

red-pine.wildlife: Minnesota's state tree; fire-adapted; seed for crossbills and squirrels

red-trillium.wildlife: Smells of carrion and is fly-pollinated; also called stinking benjamin

reed-canary-grass.wildlife: INVASIVE in Minnesota wetlands. Forms dense monocultures that exclude everything else

river-birch.wildlife: Peeling cinnamon bark; the birch that resists bronze birch borer; catkins for birds

rough-blazing-star.wildlife: The dry-prairie liatris; late nectar when little else is open

sensitive-fern.wildlife: Dies at the first frost, hence the name; bead-like fertile fronds persist all winter

serviceberry.wildlife: One of the first trees to bloom; June fruit for birds and people; excellent fall color

shooting-star.wildlife: Buzz-pollinated - bumble bees vibrate the pollen loose; goes dormant by midsummer

showy-goldenrod.wildlife: Upright plume, clump-forming rather than running - the well-behaved garden goldenrod

side-oats-grama.wildlife: Seed spikelets hang from one side of the stem; host to several skippers

silver-maple.wildlife: Floodplain tree; earliest large seed crop of the year; cavities for wood ducks and owls

skunk-cabbage.wildlife: Generates its own heat and melts through snow; the first bloom of the Minnesota year

sky-blue-aster.wildlife: Clear blue rays on dry prairie; important late nectar

smooth-blue-aster.wildlife: Waxy blue-green foliage; heavy bee and butterfly use into October

smooth-brome.wildlife: NON-NATIVE. Planted for forage; now one of the worst invaders of remnant prairie

smooth-sumac.wildlife: Scarlet fall color; fuzzy red fruit clusters are late-winter emergency bird food

sneezeweed.wildlife: Late yellow bloom for wet ground; named for snuff, not for hay fever

snow-trillium.wildlife: Minnesota's earliest trillium, often blooming in snow; a state species of concern

soft-rush.wildlife: Round green stems in tight clumps; core bioswale plant; cover for wetland wildlife

soft-stem-bulrush.wildlife: Nesting cover for marsh birds; seed for waterfowl; strong wave-energy buffer

solomons-seal.wildlife: Paired bells hang beneath an arching stem; blue-black fruit for birds

southern-maidenhair.wildlife: NOT a Minnesota native - a southern and tropical species of seeps and springs

spiderwort.wildlife: Each flower lasts one morning; buzz-pollinated by bumble bees

spotted-knapweed.wildlife: INVASIVE, state noxious weed. Chemically suppresses neighbors and takes over dry ground

squirrel-corn.wildlife: Spring ephemeral; yellow corn-like tubers; queen bumble bee forage

staghorn-sumac.wildlife: Velvety antler-like stems; red fruit holds all winter for birds

stiff-goldenrod.wildlife: Flat-topped heads on stiff stems; tolerates heavy clay; strong late nectar

sugar-maples.wildlife: The maple-basswood forest dominant; sap for syrup; orange-red fall color

sun-sedge.wildlife: Dry-prairie and savanna sedge; very early green-up

swamp-aster.wildlife: Late nectar for wet ground; purple-tinged stems

swamp-milkweed.wildlife: Monarch host; the best-behaved milkweed for gardens, and it takes normal garden soil too

swamp-white-oak.wildlife: Tolerates both flooding and compacted urban soil; acorns for waterfowl and mammals

sweetgrass.wildlife: Sacred to many Native nations and braided for ceremony; vanilla scent when dried

switchgrass.wildlife: Airy seed clouds; excellent winter cover and seed for birds

tamarack.wildlife: The conifer that drops its needles - gold in October; bog specialist

topeka-purple-coneflower.wildlife: A rare southern-Plains coneflower; not part of the Minnesota native flora

trout-lily.wildlife: Mottled leaves like a brook trout; colonies can be centuries old; early bee forage

tussock-sedge.wildlife: Builds raised pedestals that shelter frogs and nesting birds; the sedge-meadow keystone

virginia-bluebells.wildlife: Pink buds open sky blue; queen bumble bee forage; dormant by July

virginia-creeper.wildlife: Scarlet fall color; blue fruit for birds. Five leaflets - not poison ivy's three

virginia-waterleaf.wildlife: Leaves look water-stained in spring; good early nectar; spreads to fill shade

water-milfoil.wildlife: NATIVE northern milfoil - cover for fish. Distinguish from invasive Eurasian water-milfoil

white-ash.wildlife: Purple fall color; host to several sphinx moths; devastated by emerald ash borer

white-baneberry.wildlife: White berries with black dots on red stalks - doll's eyes. TOXIC to people

white-birch.wildlife: Paper bark; host to over 300 caterpillar species; catkins and seed for redpolls

white-oak.wildlife: Sweet acorns ripen in one year and are preferred by wildlife; can live 300+ years

white-pine.wildlife: Minnesota's tallest native tree; nesting for eagles and herons; seed for crossbills

white-prairie-clover.wildlife: Nitrogen fixer; the white companion to purple prairie clover; strong bee plant

white-sage.wildlife: Silver foliage; wind-pollinated; used ceremonially by many Native nations

white-snakeroot.wildlife: Late shade nectar. TOXIC - historically caused milk sickness through cows' milk

white-spruce.wildlife: Dense winter cover; seed for crossbills, chickadees and red squirrels

white-turtlehead.wildlife: The sole larval host for Baltimore checkerspot butterfly; bumble-bee pollinated

white-water-lily.wildlife: Fragrant; beetle-pollinated; pads shelter fish and frogs; seed and rhizome for waterfowl

whorled-milkweed.wildlife: Monarch host; the latest-blooming milkweed; needle-fine whorled leaves

wild-bergamot.wildlife: Perhaps the most generous pollinator plant in Minnesota - bees, moths, hummingbirds, butterflies

wild-blueberry.wildlife: Buzz-pollinated by bumble bees; fruit for birds, bears and people

wild-celery.wildlife: Canvasback ducks are named for feeding on it; core lake food plant

wild-columbine.wildlife: Red nodding spurs built for ruby-throated hummingbirds arriving in May

wild-geranium.wildlife: Reliable pink woodland bloom; seed capsules fling seed several feet

wild-ginger.wildlife: Flowers hidden at ground level and pollinated by beetles and flies; excellent shade groundcover

wild-grape.wildlife: Fruit for over 100 bird species; bark strips used by nesting birds

wild-lupine.wildlife: The ONLY larval host for the endangered Karner blue butterfly; nitrogen fixer

wild-onion.wildlife: Nodding pink umbels; edible; good late-summer bee forage

wild-parsnip.wildlife: INVASIVE, state noxious weed. Sap plus sunlight causes severe burns and blistering

wild-plum.wildlife: Clouds of fragrant white bloom before leaves; fruit for wildlife and jelly; forms thickets

wild-rice.wildlife: Manoomin - sacred to the Ojibwe and central to their treaty rights; critical waterfowl food

wild-rose.wildlife: Simple pink five-petaled flowers; hips persist all winter for birds

wild-strawberry.wildlife: Native groundcover; small intensely flavored fruit; larval host for grizzled skipper relatives

yarrow.wildlife: Flat landing pads for small bees, wasps and beneficial flies; very long bloom

yellow-birch.wildlife: Curling bronze bark; twigs smell of wintergreen; long-lived northern hardwood

yellow-pond-lily.wildlife: Cup-shaped yellow flowers; rhizomes eaten by muskrat and beaver; pads shelter fish

zigzag-goldenrod.wildlife: Zigzagging stem; one of the few goldenrods for real shade; late woodland nectar

canada-milk-vetch.wildlife: Nitrogen fixer; nectar for long-tongued bees; seed pods rattle when dry

ground-plum.wildlife: Nitrogen fixer; plump edible pods sit right on the ground; dry-prairie specialist

large-flowered-bellwort.wildlife: Drooping twisted yellow bells; ant-dispersed seed; rich-woods indicator

nodding-fescue.wildlife: One of the few native woodland grasses; arching nodding seed heads

partridge-pea.wildlife: Nitrogen-fixing annual; extrafloral nectaries feed ants and wasps; seed for quail and songbirds

poverty-oat-grass.wildlife: Tolerates the poorest dry soils; early cool-season bunchgrass

showy-lady-slipper.wildlife: Minnesota's state flower. Protected - never dig or pick. Can take 16 years to first bloom

spring-beauty.wildlife: Spring ephemeral; pink-striped petals; supported by a specialist mining bee

white-trout-lily.wildlife: Mottled leaves; vast slow-growing colonies; early forage for emerging bees

wood-anemone.wildlife: Spring ephemeral carpet; single white flower above a whorl of leaves

blue-orchard-mason-bees.needs: Hollow stems, woodpecker holes or bee blocks to nest in; mud to seal cells; early-blooming trees and shrubs
blue-orchard-mason-bees.where: Statewide; common in orchards and gardens with nesting cavities
blue-orchard-mason-bees.note: Far more efficient at pollinating fruit trees than honeybees - a few hundred can do the work of thousands of honeybees

european-honeybee.status: INTRODUCED - not native to North America
european-honeybee.needs: Managed hives; large continuous nectar flows
european-honeybee.where: Managed colonies statewide; feral colonies uncommon in Minnesota winters
european-honeybee.note: Brought from Europe in the 1600s. Valuable for agriculture, but competes with native bees for forage and can spread disease to wild bumble bees

the-monarch-butterfly.status: Native; IUCN listed, candidate for US listing
the-monarch-butterfly.needs: Milkweed (Asclepias) for caterpillars - nothing else will do; nectar plants through September for the migrating generation
the-monarch-butterfly.where: Statewide; prairies and roadsides of western and southern Minnesota are core breeding habitat
the-monarch-butterfly.note: The generation that leaves Minnesota in fall flies up to 3,000 miles to central Mexico

emerald-ash-borer.status: INVASIVE - introduced from Asia, first found in Minnesota in 2009
emerald-ash-borer.needs: Ash trees (Fraxinus) - larvae girdle the tree by feeding under the bark
emerald-ash-borer.where: Confirmed in most of southern and central Minnesota and spreading
emerald-ash-borer.note: Minnesota has around one billion ash trees, the most of any state. Do not move firewood
